The Antlered sculpin Enophrys diceraus is a cold-water cottid found throughout the North Pacific, and its early life stages reflect a particularly slow developmental trajectory. Following a spawning event, females deposit demersal, adhesive eggs that are guarded by the male parent until the fertilised ova complete their development. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva emerges at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth being only 0.0072 grams [Wwb = 0.0072 grams]. This minute larval mass, comparable to that of other cottids with similar egg diameters, necessitates a prolonged yolk-dependent period before the onset of exogenous feeding. The larval stage is wholly dependent on the endogenous reserves provided by the large, yolk-laden egg, and the duration of this lecithotrophic phase is strongly mediated by ambient temperature. All embryonic and early larval development in this species occurs under the consistent, cold thermal regime of the nearshore benthic environment, which is typically near 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C] during the incubation period. This low temperature dramatically slows metabolic processes, extending the time required for yolk absorption and delaying the critical transition to active feeding, a strategy that aligns with the slow life-history pace typical of high-latitude sculpins.

Growth and maturation in Enophrys diceraus proceed slowly, consistent with the cold-water regime the species inhabits. Females reach sexual maturity at a total length of 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 30 grams [Wwp = 30 grams]. Continued somatic growth thereafter carries individuals to an ultimate total length of 32 cm [Li = 32 cm] and a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 760 grams [Wwi = 760 grams]. Under the same thermal regime of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for the species is 5110 days [am = 5110 days], a longevity consistent with the slow-paced life history typical of cold-water cottids.
